q: משה בן 71 עם סוכרת סוג 2 מטופל באינסולין. השבוע היו לו 2 אפיזודות היפוגליקמיה עם תסמינים. איזה מהבאים נכון לגבי נהיגה?
o: יכול להמשיך לנהוג אם נושא גלוקוז ברכב
צריך להפסיק נהיגה זמנית עד לייצוב הסוכרת
יכול לנהוג רק נסיעות קצרות מתחת ל-30 דקות
נהיגה מותרת רק אחרי בדיקת סוכר לפני כל נסיעה
explanation:
אירועים רפואיים זמניים שעלולים לסכן נהיגה מחייבים **הימנעות מנהיגה עד להתייצבות**, ולא הסתפקות באמצעי זהירות חלקי. היישום לאירועי ההיפוגליקמיה החוזרים בשאלה הוא הסקה מעקרון זה: תחילה מייצבים את המצב ומעריכים מחדש את הסיכון, ורק אז דנים בחזרה לנהיגה (חוזר 6/2023, עמ׳ 3–4).
"עליו להימנע מנהיגה עד להתייצבות מצבו הרפואי" (עמ׳ 3).

**א. יכול להמשיך לנהוג אם נושא גלוקוז ברכב.** שגויה, נשיאת גלוקוז אינה מוכיחה שהמצב התייצב; לפי עקרון החוזר, אמצעי עזר אינו מחליף הימנעות מנהיגה בתקופת סיכון זמנית. זהו יישום לתרחיש (עמ׳ 3–4).
**ב. צריך להפסיק נהיגה זמנית עד לייצוב הסוכרת.** נכונה, זו האפשרות שמיישמת את עקרון ההמתנה להתייצבות לפני חזרה לנהיגה, בעקבות האירועים החוזרים המתוארים בשאלה (עמ׳ 3–4).
**ג. יכול לנהוג רק נסיעות קצרות מתחת ל-30 דקות.** שגויה, קיצור הנסיעה אינו קובע שהמצב הרפואי התייצב. זו הסקה מהתנאי הרפואי שבחוזר, שאינו מוחלף בתנאי של מרחק או משך נסיעה (עמ׳ 3–4).
**ד. נהיגה מותרת רק אחרי בדיקת סוכר לפני כל נסיעה.** שגויה, בדיקה לפני הנסיעה אינה כשלעצמה הוכחה להתייצבות לאחר אירועים חוזרים. זו הסקה מהצורך בהערכת המצב והסיכון הפרטניים (עמ׳ 3–4).

מקור: משרד הבריאות, חוזר מנכ״ל 6/2023, עמ׳ 3–4, סעיפים 7, 9–11.
ref: משרד הבריאות, חוזר המנהל הכללי 6/2023: הגדרה מחדש של חובת ההודעה על נהגים עם מצבי בריאות העלולים לסכן את עצמם וזולתם

q: קשישה בת 78 מאושפזת ביחידה לטיפול נמרץ. בתה שואלת על מצבה הרפואי ודורשת לדעת את כל הפרטים. למטופלת אין ייפוי כוח או הוראות מוקדמות. איך יש לנהוג?
o: למסור לבת את מלוא המידע מפני שקרבת משפחה מקנה גישה לרשומה
לבדוק תחילה אם המטופלת הסכימה למסירת מידע לבתה
למסור לבת מידע כללי ללא בירור הסכמה מפני שמידע כללי אינו סודי
לדרוש מהמשפחה ייפוי כוח כתנאי לקבלת הסכמה ישירה מן המטופלת
explanation:
**סודיות רפואית** חלה גם כשבן משפחה מבקש את המידע. החוק מתיר מסירה לאחר כאשר המטופל הסכים לכך, ולכן תחילה מבררים את רצונה של המטופלת; האשפוז בטיפול נמרץ והיעדר ייפוי כוח אינם כשלעצמם הסכמה למסירה לבת. זהו יישום של סעיפים 19 ו־20, עמ׳ PDF 18 ו־19.
"המטופל נתן את הסכמתו למסירת המידע הרפואי;" (סעיף 20(א)(1), עמ׳ PDF 18).

**א. למסור לבת את מלוא המידע מפני שקרבת משפחה מקנה גישה לרשומה.** שגויה, קרבת משפחה לבדה אינה ההסכמה הנדרשת, וגם לבת אין גישה אוטומטית לכל המידע; המסירה מוגבלת למידה הנדרשת (סעיפים 19 ו־20, עמ׳ PDF 18 ו־19).
**ב. לבדוק תחילה אם המטופלת הסכימה למסירת מידע לבתה.** נכונה, זהו בירור הבסיס החוקי למסירת מידע לבת, ולא הנחה שהבת רשאית לקבלו מכוח קרבתה (סעיף 20(א)(1), עמ׳ PDF 18).
**ג. למסור לבת מידע כללי ללא בירור הסכמה מפני שמידע כללי אינו סודי.** שגויה, הסודיות חלה על כל מידע הנוגע למטופלת, ולכן הכותרת מידע כללי אינה פוטרת מבירור ההסכמה (סעיף 19, עמ׳ PDF 18).
**ד. לדרוש מהמשפחה ייפוי כוח כתנאי לקבלת הסכמה ישירה מן המטופלת.** שגויה, הסכמת המטופלת עצמה היא עילה מפורשת למסירה; אין בסעיף זה דרישה לייפוי כוח כתנאי לקבלתה (סעיף 20(א)(1), עמ׳ PDF 18).

מקור: חוק זכויות החולה, סעיפים 19 ו־20, עמ׳ PDF 18 ו־19.
ref: חוק זכויות החולה, תשנ״ו-1996 · PDF pp.18–19, sections 19–20
label: Source: חוק זכויות החולה, תשנ״ו-1996 · PDF pp.18–19, sections 19–20

q: What does overflow fecal incontinence that resembles diarrhea represent, and what finding should guide its treatment?
o: Watery leakage around impacted stool, calling for clearance of the impaction
Watery leakage indicating an empty colon, calling for reduced laxative use
Watery leakage indicating rapid transit, calling for suppression of bowel movements
Watery leakage excluding stool retention, calling for deferral of rectal assessment
explanation:
**Overflow fecal incontinence** can be mistaken for diarrhea even though retained stool is the underlying problem. Hazzard states, "Fecal impaction must be ruled out in the presence of fecal soiling or incontinence"; a large, firm rectal impaction is manually evacuated before enemas or suppositories (pp. 1363, 1376).

**A. Watery leakage around impacted stool, calling for clearance of the impaction.** Correct, the source links watery leakage to overflow and requires evaluation for impaction; identified impaction needs clearance (pp. 1363, 1376).
**B. Watery leakage indicating an empty colon, calling for reduced laxative use.** Wrong, watery leakage does not establish an empty colon; it is specifically described as a presentation in which impaction must be excluded (p. 1363).
**C. Watery leakage indicating rapid transit, calling for suppression of bowel movements.** Wrong, inference from the impaction treatment: suppressing bowel movements does not address the retained mass that requires evacuation (pp. 1363, 1376).
**D. Watery leakage excluding stool retention, calling for deferral of rectal assessment.** Wrong, the source directs assessment for fecal impaction when leakage is present, rather than treating leakage as evidence against retention (p. 1363).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1363, 1376.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp. 1363, 1376

q: A healthy 72-year-old man takes lisinopril for hypertension and exercises regularly. He asks whether supplements advertised as targeting aging pathways will help him live longer. What should guide your advice?
o: Recommend the supplement on the strength of its proposed biological mechanism
Defer supplement use pending rigorous clinical data and FDA review
Recommend the supplement on the strength of its over-the-counter availability
Recommend the supplement on the strength of claims from an unregulated clinic
explanation:
**Biological plausibility** does not establish clinical effectiveness or safety. Hazzard cautions: "A plausible link to mechanisms of aging does not mean an intervention will be effective or risk-free" (p. 602). Clinical judgment must take account of the absence of rigorous clinical data and FDA approval (p. 602).

**A. Recommend the supplement on the strength of its proposed biological mechanism.** Wrong, a proposed link to aging mechanisms does not establish effectiveness or freedom from risk (p. 602).
**B. Defer supplement use pending rigorous clinical data and FDA review.** Correct, this follows the source's caution about using these substances ahead of rigorous clinical data and FDA approvals (p. 602).
**C. Recommend the supplement on the strength of its over-the-counter availability.** Wrong, over-the-counter agents are included in the source's warning; availability does not provide the missing clinical evidence (p. 602).
**D. Recommend the supplement on the strength of claims from an unregulated clinic.** Wrong, the source distinguishes unregulated clinics from carefully controlled and regulated clinical trials (pp. 602-603).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 602, 603.

q: An 84-year-old woman who lives alone and manages her medications was independent in basic ADLs until three days ago. Her daughter finds her acutely confused and inattentive. Temperature is 37.1°C, heart rate 88/min, blood pressure 108/62 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20/min. She is oriented to person only and repeatedly asks when her husband, who died two years ago, will arrive. Medications include donepezil 10 mg, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, and zolpidem 10 mg nightly, started one week ago. Which interpretation should guide the initial assessment?
o: Progression of dementia; focus on the chronic cognitive trajectory
Delirium; review zolpidem and investigate other acute contributors
Primary depression; focus on mood before evaluating acute illness
Primary psychosis; focus on delusions before evaluating acute illness
explanation:
**Acute inattention and disorientation** require assessment for delirium. Hazzard contrasts delirium developing over hours to days with the insidious course of dementia and lists zolpidem among drugs that may induce or worsen delirium (pp. 883, 885). The new exposure warrants review rather than proving a sole cause: “The etiology of delirium is usually multifactorial” (p. 881).

**A. Progression of dementia; focus on the chronic cognitive trajectory.** Wrong, sudden inattention is not explained simply by an insidious dementia trajectory (pp. 883, 885).
**B. Delirium; review zolpidem and investigate other acute contributors.** Correct, this recognizes delirium and treats the new hypnotic as a possible contributor while preserving the broader evaluation (pp. 881, 883, 885).
**C. Primary depression; focus on mood before evaluating acute illness.** Wrong, the source advises managing possible delirium and seeking precipitants when uncertain, rather than deferring medical assessment for a mood diagnosis (p. 886).
**D. Primary psychosis; focus on delusions before evaluating acute illness.** Wrong, delusional symptoms can occur in delirium; acute inattention and disorientation require delirium assessment before a primary psychiatric attribution (pp. 883, 886).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 883, 881, 886.

q: A 78-year-old man requires analgesia after hip-fracture surgery. The team wants to reduce opioid exposure while maintaining pain treatment. Which principle is consistent with enhanced recovery after surgery?
o: Rely on increasing the opioid dose as the central analgesic strategy
Postpone analgesic treatment to reduce exposure to medicines after surgery
Combine analgesic approaches while minimizing opioid use after surgery
Use one analgesic mechanism to reduce the range of postoperative medicines
explanation:
**Enhanced recovery after surgery** uses multimodal analgesia to minimize opioid use while treating postoperative pain. Opioids still have an important role, but their adverse effects, particularly in older adults, motivate opioid-sparing approaches (p. 1062).
"The mainstay of ERAS protocols is the judicious use of multimodal analgesia." (p. 1062).

**A. Rely on increasing the opioid dose as the central analgesic strategy.** Wrong, relying on opioid escalation does not implement the opioid-sparing multimodal approach described in the source (p. 1062).
**B. Postpone analgesic treatment to reduce exposure to medicines after surgery.** Wrong, the approach provides analgesia through several methods; it does not seek lower exposure by leaving postoperative pain untreated (p. 1062).
**C. Combine analgesic approaches while minimizing opioid use after surgery.** Correct, this combines the central multimodal principle with the goal of minimizing opioid use (p. 1062).
**D. Use one analgesic mechanism to reduce the range of postoperative medicines.** Wrong, restricting treatment to one mechanism misses the multimodal approach that forms the mainstay of the protocol (p. 1062).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1062.

q: A 79-year-old man with depression, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and chronic pain reports worsening mood and poor sleep six months after his wife's death. He drinks three to four glasses of wine nightly to sleep. He takes sertraline 100 mg daily, started four months ago, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, gabapentin 300 mg three times daily, and diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime. His PHQ-9 score is 22. Which approach directly addresses the two sleep self-treatments that Hazzard identifies as problematic in older adults?
o: Continue diphenhydramine and increase the evening alcohol used for sleep.
Continue alcohol for sleep and increase the bedtime diphenhydramine dose.
Stop diphenhydramine for insomnia and address the alcohol used for sleep.
Continue both sleep self-treatments while changing the antidepressant.
explanation:
**Diphenhydramine** can cause next-day sedation, delirium, decreased cognition, and urinary retention (p. 661). Hazzard states it "should not be used as a primary treatment for insomnia in older patients" (p. 661). Alcohol used for sleep can disrupt later sleep and worsen sleep difficulties, so both exposures need attention; this does not substitute for assessment of his depression (p. 661).

**A. Continue diphenhydramine and increase the evening alcohol used for sleep.** Wrong, this retains diphenhydramine and increases alcohol despite both being problematic sleep treatments (p. 661).
**B. Continue alcohol for sleep and increase the bedtime diphenhydramine dose.** Wrong, increasing diphenhydramine exposure conflicts with the advice against using it for insomnia and leaves the alcohol-related sleep problem unaddressed (p. 661).
**C. Stop diphenhydramine for insomnia and address the alcohol used for sleep.** Correct, this addresses both exposures named in the question and the source (p. 661).
**D. Continue both sleep self-treatments while changing the antidepressant.** Wrong, changing an antidepressant while leaving these exposures intact does not address the two problematic sleep self-treatments (p. 661).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 661.

q: A care-home resident with dementia and behavioral problems is assessed for possible pain. What was the first step in the empiric stepwise pain-treatment protocol described in Hazzard?
o: Begin an initial therapeutic trial of acetaminophen
Begin an initial therapeutic trial of an antipsychotic
Begin an initial therapeutic trial of an opioid
Wait for a detailed verbal description of the pain
explanation:
**Pain treatment in dementia** can be approached empirically when behavioral symptoms raise concern for pain. In the nursing-home trial described by Hazzard, the first step was acetaminophen; opioids were an option for nonresponders, and antipsychotics were not recommended as first-line treatment for behavioral symptoms (p. 1048).
"Most patients were treated with the first step of the protocol, acetaminophen." (p. 1048).

**A. Begin an initial therapeutic trial of acetaminophen.** Correct, acetaminophen was the initial step in the protocol, and most patients in the trial were treated at that step (p. 1048).
**B. Begin an initial therapeutic trial of an antipsychotic.** Wrong, the source recommends against antipsychotics as first-line treatment for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia and identifies acetaminophen as the first pain-treatment step (p. 1048).
**C. Begin an initial therapeutic trial of an opioid.** Wrong, opioids were considered for patients who did not respond, rather than as the initial step (p. 1048).
**D. Wait for a detailed verbal description of the pain.** Wrong, the described approach is an empiric pain-treatment protocol and also mentions PAINAD as an assessment aid; a detailed verbal report is not the stated first step (p. 1048).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1048.
ref: Hazzard Ch 67 — PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An older patient develops delirium after admission for myocardial infarction and coronary catheterization. Several medications were started together. Which approach to evaluating medication contributions follows Hazzard?
o: Review all medications and the timing of changes alongside the medical evaluation
Attribute delirium to the new antiplatelet drug and change it before reviewing medications
Attribute delirium to the new statin and reduce it before evaluating other causes
Attribute delirium to the new beta-blocker and replace it before the general examination
explanation:
**A complete medication review** is part of delirium assessment. Hazzard also calls for the chronology of recent changes and evaluation for underlying illness; the stem does not establish which newly started drug caused the delirium. (p. 885)
"A complete medication review, including over-the-counter medications, is critical." (p. 885)
"Historical data including intercurrent illnesses, recent adjustments in medications, the possibility of withdrawal from alcohol, other substances, or medications, and pertinent environmental changes may elucidate precipitating factors of delirium." (p. 885)

**A. Review all medications and the timing of changes alongside the medical evaluation.** Correct, this combines the complete medication review with chronology and investigation of medical precipitants. (p. 885)
**B. Attribute delirium to the new antiplatelet drug and change it before reviewing medications.** Wrong, the stem does not establish this drug as the cause, and selecting it in advance bypasses the complete review recommended by the source. (p. 885)
**C. Attribute delirium to the new statin and reduce it before evaluating other causes.** Wrong, the stem does not establish this drug as the cause, and selecting it in advance bypasses assessment for other medication and medical contributors. (p. 885)
**D. Attribute delirium to the new beta-blocker and replace it before the general examination.** Wrong, the stem does not establish this drug as the cause, and the source calls for examination as well as a complete medication review. (p. 885)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 885.

q: איזה מהשינויים הפיזיולוגיים מתרחש בלב המזדקן?
o: תאי קיצוב ב-AV NODE יורדים בשיעור של מעל 90% עם כניסת שומן במקומו
הקרדיומיוציטים קטנים והופכים רגישים יותר לסטרס מכני
הזדקנות מעלה יכולת של ה-SARCOPLASMIC RETICULUM לצבור ולשמור סידן
פיברוזיס דיפוזי נצפה במיוקרדיום לאור הצטברות של קולגן אינטרסטיציאלי
explanation:
The aging heart develops **diffuse interstitial fibrosis** from collagen accumulation, increasing myocardial stiffness and contributing to impaired diastolic filling. Remaining cardiomyocytes enlarge as cells are lost, and reduced sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium handling slows relaxation (pp. 1116-1117).

**A. More than 90% loss of AV-node pacemaker cells with fatty replacement.** Wrong, the source identifies pacemaker-cell loss in the sinoatrial node and fibrosis in the atrioventricular node; it does not support the AV-node statement in this option (p. 1116, Table 73-1).
**B. Cardiomyocytes become smaller and more sensitive to mechanical stress.** Wrong, the remaining myocytes increase in size rather than shrink; the source describes hypertrophy in the setting of age-related cell loss (p. 1116).
**C. Aging increases the sarcoplasmic reticulum's ability to accumulate and retain calcium.** Wrong, that capacity decreases. Reduced calcium reuptake and reduced SERCA content impede relaxation (p. 1117).
**D. Diffuse myocardial fibrosis from interstitial collagen accumulation.** Correct, this is the structural change described in the source; the thicker collagen network increases myocardial rigidity and can alter diastolic filling (p. 1117).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1116-1117, Chapter 73.
